text: 8:10 a.m. You’ve been added to a new chat called “Project Phoenix.” 46 people, and nobody explains what the project is. 80 messages already. Read from the start?
Your team lead writes “Hi” and disappears into a meeting for an hour. Nothing more. All hour you replay your mistakes of the week. Reply right away?
Morning tradition in the department’s off-topic chat: everyone posts a photo of their breakfast. Today you’ve only got a stale cracker from your desk drawer. Join in?
You accidentally reacted with a clown emoji to the boss’s message about the quarter kickoff. You can remove it, but he’s already online. What now?
right: Joke about the circus of plans

text: Vika sends you a four-minute voice message. You’re on a packed bus with no headphones. Hold the phone to your ear like it’s the nineties?
A morning argument in the team chat: who left a window open overnight? Now a pigeon lives in the office. It was your window. Confess?
Before stand-up the team lead wants a status in the chat by template: “Yesterday / Today / Blockers.” Yesterday you mostly looked for the right folder. What do you write?
While looking for the work chat you accidentally post in your apartment building’s chat: “Colleagues, who’s doing the report today?” Neighbors are already replying. Explain?
In the intern chat someone asks if it’s okay to come in at 9:15. You know it is, but the boss is in this chat too. Answer?
The messenger updated overnight, and all your chat folders vanished. 120 conversations all jumbled. Sort them again?
Timur writes: “Are you in the office? Come over.” Going means three floors of stairs. Texting back means looking lazy. Your choice?
At 8:30 someone greeted the department with a coffee sticker for Monday. Below it, twenty identical stickers. Add yours?
The group lead wants you to set your messenger status to “at my desk” and update it every half hour. How do you take it?
A new bot in the work chat asks every morning, “How’s your mood from 1 to 10?” and shows management the average. What do you answer?
In the team chat Dasha asks if anyone’s seen her green mug. Your mug seems to be green too. And it has your tea in it. Check?
left: Check the bottom of the mug

text: The “Where are we eating” chat is collecting votes at 9 a.m. Four options, all the same shawarma place. Vote?
The boss sent you a link with no message. It leads to a 70-page document. Ask what he needs from you?
For two hours the project chat has been debating a button color. The vote is stuck on “blue vs. light blue.” You know the client will decide anyway. Say so?
Your team lead writes “ok” in the chat. He used to always write “ok, thanks.” Without “thanks” it sounds like a verdict. Check if everything’s fine?
Ilya answers every message forty minutes later, always with one word: “checking.” You need an answer in ten. What do you do?
You posted a screenshot to the team chat with your browser tabs visible. One reads “How to ask for a raise after one month.” Delete it?
A coworker posted a long message with a question at the very end. Everyone hit “like,” but nobody answered. Be the first to reply?
Your manager reacts to every message of yours with the “eyes” emoji. Is that “I see,” “I’m watching” or “what have you done”? Ask?
A message: “Can you give me a call?” You hate phone calls, and it’s from a coworker in the next department. Call back?
You post a complaint about the long planning meeting in the “Smoke Break” chat. A second later you realize it’s the “Planning Meeting” chat. The boss is typing...
Marina writes every message IN ALL CAPS. Even “THANKS.” You flinch every time. Gently tell her?
In the middle of a serious discussion, a photo of you from the office party lands in the project chat: someone tagged you by mistake. You’re wearing a tinfoil crown. How do you react?
Kirill drops a spreadsheet called “final_final_really_final2.xlsx” in the chat and asks you to check it. There were four finals before it. Compare them all?
You sent the boss a message and spotted a typo: instead of “my bonus” you wrote “my bosom.” He’s already read it. Fix it?
Coworkers started a cat GIF marathon in the chat. Thirty GIFs in ten minutes, and you have an urgent task. Leave the chat?
A client added you on his messenger and wrote on Saturday: “Just a question for the future.” It’s Tuesday, and you only just remembered. Reply?
Interns are sharing salaries in their chat. Someone makes $100 more than you for the same work. Message the boss?
Zhenya messages you on four apps at once: “Are you seeing this?” You aren’t, but now you’re scared to open any of them. Open one?
A pinned message in the chat: “All questions in threads only.” You’ve replied outside the thread twice now. The moderator threatens a ban. Shape up?
At 1:05 the boss writes: “Where are you?” You’re at lunch in the next room. It’s your legit lunch break, but the tone is unclear. How do you reply?
You post a meme in the “Office Memes” chat. Silence. A minute later someone else posts the same meme and everyone laughs. Claim credit?
The secretary forwards 14 files to the work chat one by one, each captioned “here.” You need the sixth. Which one is the sixth — unknown.
7:40 p.m. Your team lead writes in the team chat: “We’ll discuss tomorrow.” No context. It’ll be a long night. Ask what about?
Friday evening. A coworker posted a “quick” voice message in the team chat — twelve minutes about the quarterly plan. Listen?
9 p.m. You see the boss is online. He sees you’re online. You both pretend not to see each other. Who blinks first?
The “Friday Bar” chat has six people signed up and a table booked. You wanted to go home and watch your show. They tagged you: “You in?”
At 10:30 p.m. Lyosha sends a deadline meme captioned “This is us.” It’s funny, but you’re already in bed. Reply?
6:55 p.m. Someone in the project chat writes: “Who last touched the budget file?” You did. A minute ago. Confess?
At 8:15 p.m. the boss sent a message and immediately deleted it. All that’s left: “Message deleted.” What it said torments you all evening.
In the evening you accidentally send a quarterly sales spreadsheet to your kid’s class parents’ chat. The parents politely congratulate you on the revenue. Delete it?
You want to leave at 6:00, but the boss’s status has said “typing...” for five minutes. Stay and wait, or close the laptop?
Nastya writes late in the evening: “Still up? Can I take your task tomorrow and you take mine?” Her task is clearly worse. Agree?
On your way out you hit “Leave group” instead of “Mute” in the department chat. A notice appears: “User has left the chat.”
right: Let it stand as a manifesto

text: An evening notification: the boss added you to a chat called “Weekends Are Workdays Too (kidding).” The parentheses don’t reassure you. Join?
At 11:10 p.m. a delivery bot posts in the main work chat: “Your pizza is at the door.” It’s your order number. The department perks up. What now?
right: Delete it, go to the door

text: Every evening Gosha from the next department forwards you “interesting articles” on productivity. No time to read them: your productivity is suffering. Tell him?
After hours the chat is discussing birthday gifts for the boss. You’re asked to write the card text “from everyone.” Take it on?
Your first email to an external partner. You spend twenty minutes choosing between “Good afternoon,” “Hello” and “Greetings.” Time passes; the email is empty.
right: Google etiquette for half an hour

text: In the morning you see yesterday’s email went to the whole office, not one coworker. It says “I’ll be in tomorrow if I can crawl there.” What now?
The boss wants to be cc’d on all your emails. This morning you’ve sent nine, and he replied to one: “Why do I need this?” Keep going?
312 unread over the weekend. Half are newsletters, a quarter are “Re: Re: Fwd: Re.” Start from the top or the bottom?
Sveta sends an email with the subject “Question.” There’s no question inside, just an attachment “Document1.docx.” Answer a question with a question?
You’re writing to the division director and can’t pick a sign-off: “Regards,” “All the best” or “Have a great day!” Which one?
HR asks for a request letter “in free form, but strictly following the template.” No template attached. Write it blind?
You notice that for a week you’ve been hitting “Reply All,” which includes someone who quit long ago. It all goes to his personal email. What now?
Your team lead wants emails signed not “Regards” but “Hugs, the team!” It’s the new “brand voice.” Clients too?
Yesterday’s email from a client begins: “As I mentioned in my previous email.” You never saw a previous email. Search for it?
You forgot to turn off your out-of-office after vacation. For a week everyone’s been getting “I’m at the beach, back on the 12th.” It’s the 19th.
Your email to the boss is finished. Only one decision left: a smiley after “Thanks!”? Will it add warmth or kill your career?
Accounting sends an email with a red subject line: “IMPORTANT!!! DO NOT IGNORE!!!” Inside: a reminder to submit taxi receipts by year-end. It’s January.
Before sending, you reread the email just in case. For the eighth time. It no longer looks like English. Send it?
Rustam asks you to read his email to a client “with fresh eyes.” It has three paragraphs of apologies and not one sentence of substance. Be honest?
You accidentally replied to a client from your personal address, “kitty_92.” The client replied there: “Thanks, kitty.” Move the thread?
The boss replied to your long email with one word: “Fine.” Fine what? Fine as in good? Or “fine, we’ll talk”? Ask?
You write “report attached” and hit Send. No attachment. A minute later three people reply: “Where is it?” How do you fix it?
A client’s email addresses you by the wrong name: “Dear Ms. Olga Petrovna.” You’re not Olga Petrovna. Correct them?
An email thread has grown to 34 replies with everyone cc’d. Each one says “+1” or “Thanks.” Your inbox is drowning. Ask everyone to stop?
The project manager wants emails “shorter, but with all the details.” He sent back your two-line email as “incomplete.” Rewrite it?
You want to reply “Thanks!” to a coworker’s thank-you. But it was in a thread with forty people. Hit “Reply All”?
A partner only answers your emails after the phrase “Just a reminder about...” The third reminder already sounds like a threat. Write a fourth?
In your email to the boss, the attachment is named “Report_awful_but_its_what_we_have.xlsx.” The name is visible. Sent a minute ago.
Oleg bcc’s you on his emails so you’re “in the loop.” The recipients don’t know. Does this bother you?
The company lawyer wants a half-page disclaimer added to every client email. Your email is “Yes, that works.” Add it?
You’re writing a subject line. “Question” is too vague. “Urgent question re: Q3 procurement report” is too long. Which one?
The boss asked you to “send it to everyone.” You sent it to the department. He meant the whole company, and replies are already flying. What now?
Liza replies to your emails with voice messages on the messenger. You need a written trail for the report. What do you do?
You accidentally sent a draft that says “write something smart here.” The recipient is the CFO. He already replied: “Awaiting something smart.”
Procurement requires requests by email only, with a subject line built from an eight-field template separated by dashes. Your request is for a pen. Follow the template?
A coworker from another city emails you and signs off “Kisses.” You met him once at a conference. How do you reply?
A client sent a twenty-point email marked “Respond to each.” Sixteen points repeat each other. Respond to each?
6:30 p.m. You’ve finished an email to a client, but it’s late to send. Your email has scheduled sending. Set it for 9:00 or send now?
In the evening you reread an email you sent during the day and find “Regards, your Vasya” — a coworker’s template. You’re not Vasya.
The boss sends emails at 11 p.m. You see them at 11:01. By 11:02 you’re drafting a reply. Answer at night?
Before leaving you clean out your inbox. In the trash: “Promotion: your reply required by 6:00 p.m.” It’s 6:10.
Petya asks: “Write a vacation email for me, I’m no good at nice wording.” It’s him turning down a joint trip with his mother-in-law. Help?
You’re heading home, but an email from the director blinks in your inbox with the subject “Something about you.” Open now or have dinner in peace?
The company newsletter “Month in Review” arrives in the evening. You’re mentioned as “the employee who’s always available.” Compliment or diagnosis?
You accidentally marked an email from the boss as spam. Now all his emails go to spam. Today he asks why you’re not responding.
HR sends a survey, “Your Ideal Workday,” due by morning. You want to write “the one that’s already over.” How do you answer?
While typing an email you accidentally hit Enter in the subject line. It went out with the subject “H” and no body to a client you’ve been handling for three days.
Masha asks you to check the commas in her email to the director. There are no commas. None at all. It’s 7:20 p.m., and you have movie tickets.
You meant to hit “Forward” and hit “Reply.” The sender received: “Look how tedious he is.” The sender is him.
right: Claim it was about someone else

text: Evening, and you’ve finally reached your “Read Later” folder. 640 emails, the oldest from your first day. What now?
A partner replies to your email at 9 p.m. asking for the contract “urgently by morning.” The contract is with the lawyer, and the lawyer is asleep. Wake him?
In your sent folder you see that for a week you’ve signed off “Kind regrads.” Forty emails. Did anyone notice?
9:00 a.m., morning call. You turn on your camera and see yourself for the first time today: a perfect pillow-crease grid on your cheek. Keep the camera on?
At stand-up the team lead asks everyone to turn cameras on “for team spirit.” Behind you, laundry is drying across the entire wall. What do you do?
You joined the call before everyone else. It’s just you and the boss. Silence. He’s silently sipping coffee and staring into the camera. Say something?
At stand-up everyone gets one minute. You’re eighth and rehearsing your speech. Number three says exactly your words. What do you do?
A coworker on the morning call forgot to mute and is loudly ordering shawarma “with double garlic” by phone. Everyone’s silent. Tip him off?
The call link in the calendar leads to last year’s meeting. One person from another department is sitting there, also waiting. Wait together?
The boss on the call says: “We can’t hear you.” You talk louder. “Still can’t hear you.” You shout. The neighbors bang on the radiator.
right: Type it all in the chat

text: You discover you spent forty minutes on a call with a “potato filter” on — left over from a kids’ program this morning. Nobody said a word.
The morning meeting host asks everyone to “describe your mood in one word.” Yours is “sleepy,” but everyone says “productive.” What do you say?
Before an important call your laptop insists on “Install camera update now.” You can’t decline, only “Remind me in 5 minutes.” The call starts in 4.
A client joined the video call from his car. He’s driving and wants you to show him the presentation. You watch him stare at the screen at an intersection.
There are thirty people on the call, and only your camera is on. Everyone else is initials in circles. Turn yours off?
right: Keep your face on to the end

text: HR is running an “energizing” morning call with a workout to music. Cameras mandatory. You’re in pajama pants with a dress shirt on top. Stand up for the workout?
You join the call and everyone’s speaking English: a colleague from the overseas office is here. Your English is “London is the capital of Great Britain” level. Speak up?
The team lead records the video stand-up “for those who couldn’t make it.” Nobody will watch it, but you’re yawning on camera. Will anyone notice?
You try to share your screen but share the wrong one: a website of cats in little hats. Someone’s already typing “Send the link.”
You’ve talked for five minutes straight and suddenly notice: you’re muted. Five minutes of inspired speech lost to the void. Repeat it?
You forgot to mute and are loudly chomping an apple on the call. Everyone hears the crunch. The host says: “Someone’s hungry.” Own up?
The boss is sharing his screen and doesn’t notice a chat where he calls someone “our main slowpoke.” It might be about you. Tell him?
A two-hour call, and you forgot breakfast. Eating on camera is awkward. Turning off the camera looks suspicious. What now?
The client on the call has asked “Can you hear me?” three times, though the sound is perfect. You answer “yes” each time. He can’t hear your “yes.”
You joined the wrong meeting: it’s the board of directors, and you’re a junior who clicked the wrong link. Nobody’s noticed yet. Slip out quietly?
Mid-call your battery is dying. The charger is in another room. Someone asks you a question. The laptop says “3%.” What do you do?
During the call Rita DMs you snarky comments about the speaker. You’re laughing, and your mic is on. How do you react?
The host asks: “Any questions?” Half a minute of silence. Everyone’s waiting to see who caves first. Your question is dumb, but you have one.
You’re sharing your screen when a notification pops up: “Mom: buy bread and don’t forget you’re my little dumpling.” Everyone saw it.
The project manager holds a call that could have been an email. An hour, eight people, conclusion: “Let’s have another call.” Object?
You turn on background blur, but the app blurs you too. All that’s left on screen is your nose. Talk through your nose?
Coworkers on the call are voting in the chat. You zoned out and missed the question. Everyone’s voting “yes.” Click “yes” too?
A client on the video call asks you to “turn up the volume on the computer.” His speakers are off. He doesn’t know, and it’s hard to explain.
You leave the call, click “Leave” and say out loud: “Finally.” For some reason the app didn’t leave. Everyone heard.
Mid-call, someone at the next table in the cafe where you’re working starts a loud phone call. Your mic picks it all up. Ask them to keep it down?
On the call Denis asks the same question for the third time. Everyone’s tired. The host looks at you: “Could you explain it to him, please?” Explain?
right: Offer to go over it later

text: There’s a bookshelf behind you. A coworker asks: “What’s that yellow book?” It’s a cookbook: “100 Pasta Dishes.”
6:40 p.m. An evening call with colleagues across the ocean: it’s morning for them. You were about to have dinner. The meeting drags on. Mention it’s evening for you?
The evening call is in its third hour. You turn your camera off “for a minute” and fall asleep. You wake up to someone calling your name.
At 7 p.m. the boss says: “Let’s have a quick call.” You know his “quick”: till nine at least. Agree?
Evening team call. You’re in the kitchen, and your mom off-screen asks which one is “that awful Grisha.” Grisha is on the call.
Last call of the day. You forgot your camera was on and started changing into comfy clothes. You noticed halfway into the sweater.
On the evening call you put your headphones on in advance, but the laptop stubbornly plays sound through the speakers. Your cat is spooked by the boss’s voice.
Vlad suggests an after-work “casual video call,” everyone with pizza at home. It’s Friday, and you wanted silence. Join?
7:20 p.m. You realize you’ve worn mismatched socks on calls all day. Last call now, and you’re asked to stand up and show your “workspace.”
End of the workday. You receive a 2-hour-40-minute recording of today’s meeting with the note “Must watch.” Watch it today?
At 8 p.m. a client asks you to “quickly share your screen” and check his website. You’re already in your coat and shoes. Turn the laptop back on?
Evening video chat with family through the corporate app. Grandma asks why there’s a “Confidential” label in the corner of your screen.
You’re finally done with calls and see you never turned on Do Not Disturb. Forty messenger notifications. Open even one?
At 6:55 p.m. the team lead asks you to join a “quick 10-minute retro.” You have a run in the park at 7:00. Decline?
You leave the call, but the app froze: they can see and hear you, and you’ve gone to boil dumplings. The laptop is open in the kitchen.
8:58 a.m. Two minutes until the workday, and you’re still in bed. The laptop is on the nightstand. Working lying down — remote work or audacity?
right: Get up, wash, sit at the desk

text: First week of remote work. You realize you haven’t left your apartment in three days. Go work at the cafe around the corner?
The alarm goes off at 8:30, but you don’t have to go anywhere. You could sleep forty more minutes and make it by nine if you skip washing up. Risk it?
Remote morning. You decided to work in a dress shirt to “get in the mood.” Below: pineapple shorts. Is this what balance looks like?
In the morning you realize your “office” is the kitchen table, and your family just sat down to breakfast. Kick everyone out or work amid the oatmeal?
The team lead writes at 8:05: “At your computer yet?” The workday starts at nine. You’re in the shower, phone on the washing machine. Reply with wet hands?
The internet is crawling this morning: neighbors are downloading TV shows. Call in ten minutes. Use your phone as a hotspot?
You discover your work messenger status has said “On vacation” since last summer. Nobody mentioned it. Fix it and confess?
right: Joke about it in the chat

text: In the morning your neighbor starts renovating, drilling in time with your thoughts. You have a report to write. Where do you flee?
Today’s a hybrid day: work from home or the office. The boss is in the office; home is warm and quiet. Where do you go?
This morning your work laptop won’t turn on without its cable. The cable is at the office. You have a home computer, but working on it is forbidden.
You wake up and realize for two weeks you’ve only spoken aloud to couriers and your cat. Call coworkers “just because”?
New rule: remote workers check in by writing “Here” in the chat at 9:00 sharp. You wrote it at 9:01, and the bot already logged you as late. Dispute it?
left: Take it up with the boss

text: Morning. You sit down at your desk and realize you haven’t even washed your face, yet you’ve answered three emails. Give yourself ten minutes?
8:50. A courier buzzes the intercom with a package. Your call starts at 9:00, and he asks you to come down: “No elevator for me.” Run?
Working from home, you notice you’re on your fourth cup of coffee. It’s only 10:30. Would a fifth be too much?
1 p.m. You’re remote and decide to have a proper lunch, office-style, with soup. While it cooks, three urgent questions land in the chat. Leave the soup?
In the afternoon you learn coworkers at the office had tea and cake and “forgot” to invite you over video. Take offense?
You’re working from home with a view of the park. Sunshine, birds. People are strolling outside mid-day. Take a longer lunch walk?
The team lead checks messenger statuses. Yours switched to “Away” while you were washing dishes. The team lead writes: “All ok?”
Your laptop sits on an ironing board because it’s the only surface at the right height. The board wobbles with every word.
You realize you’ve been working from home in the same position for five hours. Your neck won’t turn. Take a stretch break or push through?
Midday, the power went out in the whole building. The laptop has an hour left; the router’s already dead. Tell the boss or wait?
The courier brings lunch while you’re on a call with a client. The doorbell sounds like a fire alarm. Answer it or not?
Coworkers at the office are discussing a task at the whiteboard, and you’re watching on video with the camera pointed at the ceiling. Ask them to turn it?
Midday, you’re tempted to put a show on “in the background.” The task is monotonous: fill in two hundred spreadsheet rows. Turn it on?
You’re working from a cafe. At the next table someone’s also on a call, discussing exactly your task. It’s your coworker from the next department.
The boss on video asks: “Where are you? Is that the sea behind you?” You’re on the balcony overlooking a reservoir. Explain?
At 3 p.m. you realize you haven’t eaten, had water or stood up. But “all messages read.” Stop and have lunch?
Anya from the office writes: “Lucky you, you’re home.” You’ve spent three days in one room with the neighbors’ renovation. Explain?
You decided to work from the park. The sun is shining right on the screen; you can’t see a thing. Your reflection looks tired. Head home?
Midday, you catch yourself having walked only between the room and the kitchen all workday. The step counter says 300. Go for a walk?
HR asks remote workers if working from home is comfortable and wants a 40-question survey filled out “for improvements.” Fill it out?
Evening, working remote. Your family calls you to watch a movie, but you promised yourself “just half an hour more” on a presentation. That half hour is entering its second hour. Give up?
6:01 p.m. You close the laptop, and a minute later your phone pings: the boss replied to an email. You could take “just a peek.”
In the evening you realize you worked all day without turning on the lights. It’s dark, and you’re sitting in the monitor’s glow. Turn on the light and wrap up?
Your roommate gets home from work and asks: “You were home all day, can you make dinner?” You were working all day.
Your day is done, but you can’t switch off: same room, same chair. Make yourself a “commute home” — a walk around the block?
At 9 p.m. you remember you didn’t log your hours in the tracker. If you don’t, the day counts as an absence. Turn the laptop on?
The team lead texts in the evening: “I see you’re online at 8 p.m. Don’t overwork!” You were online ordering pizza.
Evening, and you decide to work another hour from your favorite armchair. An hour later you realize you’ve been watching videos about building houses out of bottles.
Before bed you realize you haven’t been outside for two days. Tomorrow’s remote again. Go to the store just for the fresh air?
The boss announces that starting next month, remote work is limited to two days a week. The chat is in uproar. Speak up?
Friday evening, remote. Office coworkers went to a bar without you. You see the photos in the team chat: everyone’s laughing. Join them by video?
You’ve finished work, but the laptop insists: “Restarting in 10 minutes.” If you agree, you’ll wait for the update in the morning. What’s it going to be?
Your partner suggests going out for dinner tonight. You’ve been in loungewear all day, and the thought of wearing pants is terrifying. Go?
Evening. You notice the work tracker counted only six hours, though you sat there ten. The rest was “inactive.” File a complaint?
9:02 a.m. Morning call. The cat has lain down right on the keyboard and refuses to move. The laptop is typing “jjjjjjjj” into the team chat. Remove the cat?
right: Introduce the cat to the team

text: The dog is whining at the door: walk time. The call starts in five minutes and lasts an hour. Dash out with her?
right: She can wait till it’s over

text: Your little brother is on school break and wants to “work too.” He sits next to you and draws you a dinosaur report in your notebook. Send him away?
Mom calls at 8:45 “for a minute.” The minute is about how you’re not eating properly. Stand-up at 9:00. Interrupt Mom?
Overnight the hamster chewed through your laptop charger cable. 20% battery. Morning call with the boss in ten minutes. What now?
Your parrot has learned to say “Meeting adjourned!” Today he said it in the middle of the morning stand-up, and half the people left the call.
right: Say the parrot has a point

text: The cat climbed into the closet and fell asleep on your work shirt. It’s now covered in fur. Client call in half an hour.
Grandma is staying over and blasts the radio first thing in the morning. You ask her to turn it down; she says: “I can’t hear what you’re saying.”
At morning stand-up the dog barks at everyone who unmutes. Her favorite target is your team lead. Everyone laughs except the team lead.
left: Shut the dog in the bathroom
right: Propose the dog join the team

text: Your sister asks you to babysit her three-year-old “for a couple of hours this morning.” You have stand-up and two meetings. Agree?
On the morning call the cat walks up to the camera and shows everyone his back. In close-up. Coworkers write: “Handsome.” Remove him?
Your partner walks behind you in a towel this morning while you’re on a call. He didn’t know the camera was on. Everyone noticed.
Your nephew wants you to hear him recite a poem this morning. Right now, before your call. Listen?
The aquarium behind you is gurgling louder than usual. Someone on the call asks: “Do you have a leak somewhere?” Turn off the filter?
The cat hid in the laptop box and hisses whenever you try to reach in. The warranty card IT needs is in that box.
left: Lure the cat out with food

text: Since morning the neighbor’s dog has been howling through the wall at every ring of your laptop. He seems to think it’s a friend. Mute the ringtone?
Grandpa decided to help by “fixing the internet” this morning. Now there’s no internet at all, and Grandpa is very proud. What now?
The cat walked across the keyboard and sent your boss the message “pfrrrr.” The boss replies: “Agreed.” Explain?
Mid-presentation, the neighbor’s kid runs into the room yelling: “Your cat climbed in the toilet!” The presentation is for a client.
The dog stole your lunch off the kitchen table right as someone asked you a question on the call. You watch her run off. What do you do?
Mom video-calls at lunch and wants to see what you’re eating. You’re eating cookies over the keyboard. Show her?
During an important call the cat starts loudly throwing up somewhere off-screen. You’re leading the meeting. Interrupt?
During the day the parrot learned the phrase “What a stupid project!” and repeats it at every call. Today you have a call with the client.
left: Move the parrot to the bathroom

text: Your little nephew walks up to the camera on a call and announces: “They told me you’re all boring.” Awkward pause.
Midday, the dog decided it’s playtime and brought a ball right up to the laptop. She’s staring into your eyes and waiting. Resist?
The cat has settled on the documents you need to scan. She’s sleeping deeply and sweetly. You hate to wake her, but they’re due.
Your neighbor knocks and asks to borrow a drill. You’re on a call with your camera on. He sees you through the crack and waves at your coworkers.
left: Open up, hand over the drill

text: The cat jumped on the desk and knocked coffee onto your work papers. You need them in an hour. How do you save them?
Midday your partner is on a video call with friends in the next room. Loud laughter. You have an important meeting in five minutes.
left: Ask him to keep it down

text: Your friend’s daughter, whom you agreed to watch, asks for help with math homework. You’re working. Help?
right: Put on a cartoon for her

text: On a call you lift the cat to the camera to show your coworkers. He wriggles free and scratches your hand. Everyone sees.
Mom is visiting and decided to clean while you work. The vacuum is roaring right behind you during a call.
Your neighbor went away and left you her Pomeranian. During the day he barks at every bird outside. You have a call every hour. What now?
In the evening you leave a call, but the cat steps on a key and rejoins it. They can see you in pajamas, food in hand.
In the evening you need to finish a report, but your nephew wants to play hide-and-seek. He’s already hidden and waiting. Go find him?
The dog has been waiting for a walk since 5:30. You’re on a call till 6:30. She’s sitting by the door with the leash in her mouth. Take pity?
At 7 p.m. Mom calls asking how to send photos “to that email of yours.” You’re still in work mode. Explain?
right: Promise to show her on the weekend

text: In the evening your partner is upset: “Calls all day, and no time to talk to me.” You’re still on the laptop. Close it?
right: Ask for half an hour more

text: In the evening the cat brought you a “gift”: your computer mouse. The work one. Wireless. Chewed. Tomorrow you’ll have to explain to IT.
Grandma video-calls and wants to see your office. You’re home, and the “office” is a stool by the window. Show her?
right: Show a photo from the internet

text: You leave an evening call and see the dog chewed through the lamp cord. No light. The report isn’t done.
In the evening the neighbor’s kid you’re watching draws on your work laptop in marker. The drawing: a cat captioned “For the boss.”
Over dinner your family asks how your day went. You talk about calls, and everyone dozes off. Keep going?
In the evening the cat climbed into your work bag and fell asleep on the laptop. You have to get up early for the office tomorrow. Wake him?
In the evening Mom says she saw you in an office party photo online. She wants to know who that “cute boy next to you” is. It’s your boss.
The hamster escaped while you were on an evening call. Somewhere in the apartment: silence. Suspicious. Start the search?
In the evening the dog brings your slippers and drops them by the door. A clear hint. Take her for a walk?
8:30 a.m. Your mouse is dead. You file a support ticket. The system automatically assigns it number 48,112 and priority “Low.” Wait?
You go to the sysadmin with a question, and without looking up from his monitor he says: “File a ticket.” You’re standing three feet from him.
This morning your monitor shows everything upside down. You call support, and they ask: “Have you tried tilting your head?” Is that a joke?
left: Laugh and wait for a tech

text: The hallway printer prints only the first page of a document, then says “Paper jam” with no jam. Your contract is 12 pages.
left: Print one page at a time

text: Your request for a new keyboard has been “Pending approval” for three weeks. The “o” key on yours doesn’t work. Type without “o”?
In the morning the sysadmin goes desk to desk silently swapping everyone’s monitors for new ones. He carries off your old one, with the cat stickers. Ask to keep it?
left: Ask to keep the old one

text: The support bot replies to your ticket: “Resolved. Restart your computer.” You restarted. Not resolved. The bot closed the ticket.
You open your work laptop to a blue screen with a message in an unknown language. The report is due today. Call support?
In the morning the sysadmin asks who here “always forgets to turn off their computer.” Everyone looks at you. Your computer is glowing across the room.
You got a new laptop. It can’t see any of your folders. The IT guy says: “It’s all in the cloud.” The cloud is empty.
This morning the printer is churning out 300 copies of yesterday’s report. Someone apparently hit “Repeat.” The pile is growing. Stop it?
Support wants the ticket to include “IP address, MAC address and inventory number.” You don’t know any of the three. What do you do?
The sysadmin disabled changing wallpapers on your computers. Now everyone has a gray logo background. You had a sea view. Ask for it back?
right: Hang a sea photo on the wall

text: The office smart speaker has answered every question since morning with “Please contact tech support.” You asked the time. Call them?
Every morning support asks: “Has your problem been resolved?” It hasn’t, but you’ve learned to work around it. Click “Yes”?
Your pass doesn’t work at the turnstile this morning. The guard says: “Not my department, that’s IT.” IT is on the other side of the turnstile.
Support connects to your computer remotely. The mouse moves by itself across the screen. You watch it open the folder named “Personal.”
The sysadmin asks you to hold a cable while he crawls under the desk. Twenty minutes later you’re still holding the cable. He went to lunch.
You tell support the internet isn’t working. The reply arrives three hours later: “Please email us a screenshot of the error.”
The printer prints everything pink. You need to print a report for the director. Looks like the cyan cartridge ran out. Print in pink?
You discover tickets get handled faster if you tick “Blocking the manager’s work.” That’s not true. Tick it?
Once a month the sysadmin holds “computer cleanup day.” You’re asked to delete everything unnecessary. There are 340 files on your desktop. Start?
Your headphones died midday. Support hands out temporary ones: huge, with cat ears. There are no others. Take them?
Slava asks for help with his computer because you’re “young, you get this stuff.” You don’t get it any better than he does. Help?
Support says: “To get access to the folder, submit a request for access to the ticketing system.” You don’t have access to the ticketing system.
right: Ask a coworker to file it

text: The sysadmin praised you for the first time: “You’re the only one who reads the instructions.” Now he sends you every new instruction to proofread.
The meeting-room projector is dead. In five minutes you’re presenting to the department head. IT isn’t picking up.
Support closes your ticket with the note “Cannot reproduce.” The error reproduces for you every ten minutes. Record a video?
The sysadmin asks you to temporarily be a “tester” for a new system. It’ll add work, but they promise a thank-you in the newsletter. Agree?
The printer throws an “Insufficient memory” error. You’re printing one page with one word: “Pass.” Restart the printer?
To get support to come faster, coworkers advise writing that “something smells like burning.” They say it never fails. Try it?
Your desk phone rings, but the handset won’t lift: its cord is tangled with the monitor cable. It’s the boss calling.
The sysadmin spots a personal power strip on your desk and demands it go: “Not certified.” Your kettle runs off it.
5:55 p.m. Your computer says: “Your account will be locked in 5 minutes due to inactivity.” You’ve been active all day.
The sysadmin heads home with a parting “If anything happens, just restart.” Five minutes later everything freezes. What now?
An evening email: “Your request has been fulfilled.” It was for a new monitor. The monitor is on your coworker’s desk next to you.
In the evening your laptop stops charging. Important meeting in the morning. Support has gone home. What’s the plan?
In the evening IT posts in the team chat: “Tomorrow from 8 to 10 the server will be unavailable.” Your deadline is at 9:00. Submit today?
You’re staying late, and the sysadmin asks you to switch off “that big computer in the corner.” It’s the server. You realize this at the last moment.
In the evening you get a survey: “Rate the quality of tech support.” Your ticket still isn’t resolved. Give an honest 1?
In the evening, after everyone’s left, the printer suddenly comes to life and prints the whole day’s documents. Yours too. Including a stray “resume_new.”
The sysadmin writes at 8 p.m.: “Did you do something to your computer? Your security is disabled.” You installed a game for your lunch break.
In the evening you decide to fix the mouse yourself with a screwdriver. Inside is a little spring that shoots under the cabinet. The mouse is dead.
As you’re leaving, the laptop offers to “Check disk for errors.” It’ll take “5 minutes to 3 hours.” Click “Yes” and leave?
You’re working late, and the building’s power is shut off “as scheduled.” Your document isn’t saved. Five hours of work hang in the balance.
The sysadmin invites you to a bar tonight to celebrate the “server migration.” You don’t know what that is, but all of IT is going.
9:00 a.m. The system demands a new password: “At least 14 characters, no repeats, no dictionary words, not similar to your last 24.” You haven’t had coffee yet.
left: Come up with a real one

text: Security announced a mandatory “Cyber Hygiene” course. Twelve 20-minute video lessons and a test at the end. Due Friday.
Two-factor authentication sends codes to your work phone. Your work phone is at home; you’re at the office. Without the code you can’t log in anywhere.
Gena asks in the morning: “Can I log in from your computer? My password got locked.” This is explicitly against security rules.
A “Clean Desk” flyer lands on your desk: when leaving, clear away all papers. Papers on your desk lie in layers like an archaeological dig.
right: Shove it all in a drawer

text: A morning email from “the CEO”: “Urgently buy gift cards and send me the codes.” The signature is right; the address is odd. What do you do?
You enter your password, and the system says: “Incorrect. 2 attempts left.” You’ve confidently typed it for three days straight. Keep trying?
Security staged a “training phishing attack.” You clicked the link “You’ve won a coffee machine.” Now you’re enrolled in extra training.
In the morning you hold the door for a stranger carrying boxes. A minute later an email warning arrives: “Do not let strangers in!”
A coworker’s monitor has a sticky note with a password on it. The security officer is coming down the aisle and is about to see it. Warn your coworker?
The security officer does a morning round checking that everyone locks their computer when getting coffee. Yours is unlocked. You’re in the coffee line.
This morning the system wants to confirm login “by fingerprint.” You cut your finger slicing bread. The sensor doesn’t recognize you.
An email arrives: “Confirm your password or your mailbox will be deleted.” Perfect design, real logo. In the address, the “o” is a zero.
Morning security quiz: “What do you do if you find a flash drive in the parking lot?” A) plug it in, B) hand it in, C) throw it away. You honestly don’t know.
Security banned plugging phones into computers “to charge.” Your phone is at 3%, and the kitchen outlet is taken by the kettle.
right: Walk around with a dead phone

text: You entered your password and noticed Caps Lock was on — yet it let you in. So you’ve been typing it in caps all month. Tell IT?
Mandatory security test: 30 questions, passing score 100%. You got 29 of 30. You have to retake the whole thing.
The security officer gives a lecture and offers an example of a bad password: “Say, Fluffy2001.” That’s your password. You break out in a sweat.
Karina asks you to send her the shared folder password via messenger. Security forbids passwords in messengers. Karina needs it urgently.
A call: “This is your employer’s bank, please read me the code from the text.” The voice is polite, with call-center noise in the background.
right: Ask where they got your number

text: The security course says to change passwords everywhere you reuse one. You have one password for everything, from email to pizza orders.
Security demands everyone install an authenticator app. Your phone is old and won’t install it. What do you suggest?
After a meeting you find a flash drive labeled “Salaries 2025” in the conference room. You’re dying to look. Plug it in?
Your boss reads you his email password so you can “send one email for him.” The password is his birthday. What do you do?
The security course asks you to create a four-word “passphrase.” Your pick: “I want home right now.” Use it?
Security blocks the recipe site because it “threatens work time.” You checked it every day at lunch. Complain?
A courier at the entrance asks for your last name and job title to “deliver documents.” Nobody’s expecting any documents. Tell him?
A gamified security course: the character “Hacker Harry” tries to steal your data. Each level takes 15 minutes. There are twelve.
For some reason Tonya photographed her screen full of passwords and posted it in the team chat: “Look how organized I am!” Tell her?
The system allows reusing a password only after 24 changes. You change it 24 times in a row to get your favorite back. It’s not forbidden.
Security requires you to wear your badge around your neck, even in the cafeteria. The lanyard keeps dipping into your soup. Follow the rule?
After the security course you were chosen as the department’s “cyber hygiene ambassador.” You must remind coworkers to lock their screens. Accept?
The security test asks: “How often should you change your password?” Options: “Monthly,” “Yearly,” “When you forget it.” You honestly change it when you forget it.
5:50 p.m. The system says: “Your password expires in 1 minute.” If you don’t change it, you’ll be locked out in the morning. Your brain is fried.
In the evening you remember you never finished the security course. Tomorrow’s the last day. The course is two hours. Your show is waiting.
In the evening security sends phishing-drill results: “34% of employees clicked.” A list of names is attached. Yours is on it.
A text on your personal phone: “Your work account has been hacked, follow the link.” It’s evening, IT has gone home. Check it out?
Stas leaves early and asks you to “close his computer for him.” It’s unlocked, with his chats on screen. Close it?
As you’re leaving, the system offers to “Remember this device for 30 days.” If you click “No,” you’ll be entering codes again tomorrow. Security advises against “Yes.”
After a three-hour course you get a “Cybersecurity Expert” certificate. Mom asks if you can now hack her email password for her.
right: Explain it doesn’t work that way

text: In the evening the security officer says: “Show me where you keep your passwords.” You keep them in a notebook with kittens on it. Show him?
right: Say it’s all in your head

text: At 8 p.m. an email arrives: “Your password has expired, click here.” You’re tired and almost click. Your hand hovers over the mouse.
In the evening the authenticator app reports: “Sign-in attempt from another country.” You’re at home. Click “This wasn’t me”?
On your way out you left your pass on your desk. The guard at the exit won’t let you out: “No pass, no exit.” Go back?
In the evening you tell friends about the security course and realize all their passwords are “123456.” Start a lecture?
You enter your password in the evening, but the keyboard switched to another language layout. Three tries means lockout. One left.
8:55 a.m. You open the laptop and it shows: “Installing updates 3 of 147. Don’t turn off your computer.” Stand-up in five minutes.
The company portal was updated overnight. The “Vacation” button moved to “My Achievements → Other → Archive.” Look for it?
IT newsletter: “Starting Monday we’re switching to a new document system. Training: 6 hours of video.” Today is Friday.
right: Figure it out as you go

text: The email app updated and now groups emails “by meaning.” The boss’s email ended up under “Entertainment.”
The company is moving to a new messenger. All chats, stickers and three years of jokes stay in the old one. Copy what matters?
The new CRM version wants every client profile filled out again. You have three hundred. Fill them in right away?
This morning the laptop updated the browser, and all your saved tabs vanished. Six months of “read later.” Restore them?
IT announces: a new time-tracking system. Every 15 minutes you log what you’re doing. Your first entry: “Logging time.”
After the portal update, your profile photo was replaced with another employee’s — a bearded engineer. Now everyone messages him.
The spreadsheet app updated, and all your formulas show “#ERROR.” The report is due at 11. What now?
The new helper bot answers every question with “a useful article.” You asked how to request vacation, and it sent an article on the dangers of procrastination. Now what?
After an update your laptop is in German. Every menu, every button. You look for how to switch back, but the menus are in German too.
The calendar updated and decided you live in another time zone. All meetings shifted an hour, and you’re already late for one. What now?
This morning IT installed a new program to “improve performance.” Now your computer takes twenty minutes to boot instead of two.
The updated portal has a “thank-you wall.” Coworkers have already thanked each other. Nobody’s thanked you yet. Thank someone first?
A messenger update added read receipts. Now everyone sees you read the boss’s message at 7:02 and didn’t reply.
The new document system requires an e-signature. To get one, you must sign an application. With an e-signature.
right: Sign in pen and scan it

text: Overnight the laptop restarted itself for an update and closed your unsaved document. The app “recovered” it — a week-old version.
The new CRM shows a full-screen “Tip of the Day” with every client call. You can close it only after 10 seconds. Forty calls a day.
The portal was updated, and vacations now require a “multi-step process.” Nine steps. The last is “Approval of the approval.”
After an update, spreadsheets started auto-coloring cells “by the mood of the data.” Your report is now a rainbow. The boss loves it.
IT asks everyone to test the new system and fill out a survey: “What do you like?” You like nothing. How do you answer?
A new messenger update automatically translates all messages into “business speak.” Your “ok” became “Your proposal has been accepted for consideration.”
The new document system lost your document. Its status says: “Document exists.” Where — unknown.
The new portal requires “onboarding”: five quizzes on company history. You’ve worked here six months, but it’s mandatory.
The video-call app updated mid-call. You got kicked out. You can only rejoin after a 12-minute update.
The new CRM automatically sends clients a “Thanks for calling” email with your photo. Your passport photo. It’s embarrassing.
IT rolled out “artificial intelligence” to check reports. It flags every one of your sentences as “too long.” Rewrite?
The updated spreadsheet app opens files “read-only.” To edit, you need access granted by someone who’s on vacation.
After the update, the portal lists your title as “Senior Specialist.” You’re a junior. Fix it or let it be?
The new meeting-room booking system requires booking two days ahead. You need a room in 15 minutes for a call.
After an update, the messenger deleted all your pinned messages. They held passwords, links and Grandma’s pie recipe.
The new system requires attaching a 20-field “document card” to every document. Your document is a note: “At lunch, back at 2:00.”
Borya is thrilled with the new update and wants to show you “all the cool features.” It’ll take half an hour. Work is waiting.
IT sends the manual for the new program: 84 pages with pictures. The pictures are from the old version.
The new CRM gives clients a “loyalty score.” Your best client got “Churn risk.” He doesn’t know. Call him?
6 p.m. You close the laptop, and it shows: “Updating. Do not turn off. About 1 hour 40 minutes remaining.” You need to take it home.
right: Carry it open on the subway

text: In the evening IT announces: “Everyone install the update before 9:00 tomorrow.” It takes an hour and a half to install.
right: Install in the morning, be late

text: In the evening the portal notifies you: “You haven’t completed the mandatory course on the new system.” It’s three hours; the deadline was yesterday.
In the evening the messenger updated and turned on “status sync” for everyone. Now coworkers can see you’re listening to “Hang In There, Monday.”
In the evening the updated spreadsheet app offers “AI assistance.” You accept. The AI deletes half the report as “unnecessary.”
At home in the evening your laptop updated too and set the corporate wallpaper: “We Are One Family.” It makes home feel less cozy.
At 7:30 p.m. IT writes: “Can someone stay and test the update? We need one person.” Everyone’s silent.
In the evening the CRM sends all clients automatic “Happy Birthday!” emails. All of them at once. Nobody has a birthday today.
The company portal sends you a “Month in Review”: “You spent 82% of your time in calls.” That’s a department record.
In the evening the new document system sent all your drafts to the boss for approval. Twenty of them.
In the evening you realize the messenger sent you no notifications all day after the update. You missed 40 messages. Reply?
IT announces: the old system shuts down for good tomorrow at 8:00. You still need to export a year of your reports from it.
8:45 a.m. The boss asks you to “quickly merge a spreadsheet” for the planning meeting. It’s twelve files from different departments in different formats. Meeting at 10.
You open the department’s shared spreadsheet and see someone sorted a single column overnight without touching the others. All the data is scrambled.
In the morning Vera sends a report and asks you to “check the numbers.” The numbers are fine, but it’s all in a curly font like a greeting card. Mention the font?
You spend three hours on the weekly report every Monday. Nobody reads it: you checked — since March it’s contained “If you’re reading this, let me know.” Keep going?
This morning you discover the spreadsheet is 300 MB and takes twenty minutes to open. Inside: 40 hidden sheets named “Sheet1 (copy 17).”
The finance guy wants the report “broken down.” Broken down how, he doesn’t say. Options: by month, region, manager. Ask?
You open “Budget_final” and see the total is calculated by the formula “=5+5.” Someone “fixed it by hand.” What now?
In the morning the boss says: “I need a chart. A pretty one. So everything’s clear.” He sent no data. Make a chart out of thin air?
In the morning Margarita renamed every column in the shared spreadsheet “for convenience.” Your formulas broke. She’s proud of the result.
The report template requires a “Conclusions” field. Your data supports exactly one: “Nothing changed.” Write it honestly?
The spreadsheet asks you to “Enable macros.” Security forbids it, and without macros the file just shows “Enable macros.”
The group lead introduced a new rule this morning: all reports as PDFs, but editable. You have no idea how that’s possible.
This morning you realize the report you submitted yesterday was for last month. You opened the wrong file. The boss hasn’t read it yet.
You open the shared spreadsheet and five people are already in it. Their cursors jump across cells. Your cell keeps getting overwritten.
Finance sends your report back with the note “Off by $3.” You hunt for those three dollars across 4,000 rows.
The report needs to show “growth.” There is growth — but only if the chart starts at 98% instead of zero. Is that allowed?
In the morning the boss asks to “add one more column to the report.” An hour later: “one more.” By lunch the report has 43 columns.
This morning you find something personal in the shared spreadsheet: a birthday gift list. Your name is on the “no gift” list.
Pasha sends a report with every number highlighted in red “for emphasis.” It’s impossible to read. You have to present it to the boss.
You spent three days on a report. The boss opened it, glanced at the first page and said: “Can we get all this in one number?”
left: Boil it down to one number

text: You accidentally clicked “Delete row” in the shared spreadsheet. Gone: the row with the whole department’s salaries. You can undo it, but only if nobody saves.
The boss wants a report “like last time, only better.” He returned last time’s report with the note “Not bad.” What does “better” mean?
A 30-page report template. 28 pages fill in automatically. Two are “Analysis and Conclusions.” You’ve been staring at them for an hour.
In the pivot table it turns out “New York,” “new york” and “NYC” count as three different cities. The totals don’t add up.
Tamara asks you to teach her pivot tables. She wants to learn “in five minutes.” It took you a month.
You handed the report to the boss. An hour later he returns it with red-ink edits. There are no edits, just the words: “See for yourself.”
A formula in the spreadsheet works, but you don’t understand why. It was built by someone who quit two years ago. Touch it?
The project manager wants a “real-time dashboard.” The data arrives once a month, by email, as scans.
You find a typo in the client company’s name in the report: “Daisey LLC.” The report has already gone to the client. Call them?
right: Fix it in the next version

text: While building a report you notice a coworker’s numbers for last quarter are wrong. If you say so, he’ll get in trouble.
The boss wants a report “by lunch.” You ask which lunch. He says: “Well, mine.” He eats lunch whenever he feels like it.
Your report was sent “upstairs.” A day later the question comes back: “Who wrote this wonderful report?” Your boss replies that he did.
You’re hunting for one error in a 5,000-row spreadsheet. Found it. Fixed it. The spreadsheet says: “4,999 other errors detected.”
Mitya proposes “automating the report.” It’ll take two weeks. Right now you do it in an hour. The boss already loves the idea.
You’ve been asked to write a report on how much time the department spends on reports. The report will take three days.
You color-coded the spreadsheet rows for convenience. A coworker asks what each color means. You forgot.
Nikolai sends you a spreadsheet “for your information.” It’s forty sheets linked by formulas to your spreadsheet. Now yours is crawling.
6:30 p.m. The report is almost done. Just the chart labels left. You can no longer remember what blue means and what red means.
At 7 p.m. the boss writes: “Looked at the report. I have questions.” No questions included. It’ll be a restless night. Ask which ones?
In the evening you close the spreadsheet and forget to save. The app asks: “Save changes?” On autopilot, you click “No.”
The report is ready in the evening, but you realize: if you send it now, the boss will think you stay late. Is that good or bad?
At 8 p.m. you discover the spreadsheet has been calculating everything wrong since the start of the quarter. Tomorrow it’s being presented to management.
Yana asks you in the evening to “just take a look” at her report. It’s 60 pages. She says “there’s not much.”
In the evening you think you’ve submitted the report. But the email is stuck in the Outbox. It’s 9 p.m., and the boss already asked about it this morning.
In the evening you decided to “improve the spreadsheet a little.” Three hours later it’s beautiful, but it doesn’t work anymore.
At 6:50 p.m. the boss says: “Good report, but let’s redo it all in a different format.” It’s Friday.
Your report made it into the final presentation for the director. In the evening you see your key conclusion was cut out.
In the evening your family asks for help with the household budget in a spreadsheet. You stared at spreadsheets all day. Again?
At 6:45 p.m. the finance guy asks for “one small data export.” It takes two hours to generate. Leave it running and go?
An evening email: “Your report was chosen as the best in the department! Prepare a 30-minute presentation by morning.” Joy and terror.
In the evening, dreaming of vacation, you make a “Vacation Plan” spreadsheet. In the morning it accidentally opens on the shared screen.
8:20 a.m. You reread yesterday’s email to the boss: “Look at the report at any convenient tiem.” The boss replied “Ok,” but what if he noticed? Send a correction?
Your phone’s autocorrect turned “Good morning, Igor Petrovich” into “Good morning, Igor Pierogi.” Sent. The boss is online.
The boss replies to your email in the morning: “What is a ’quaterly report’?” One missing “r,” and you’re the center of attention.
You emailed the boss with the subject “Weekly report,” but the body says “Weakly report.” The boss forwarded it to the department with the note “Learning moment.”
In the morning you text the boss “Running 10 min late, traffic,” but autocomplete adds “love you.” You can’t delete it — already read.
You meant to write the boss “OK, will do,” but your finger slipped: “OK, will do. Probably.” He’s already typing a reply.
In your email to the director you botched the grammar: “Please considering my proposal.” Sent. The director is famous for loving grammar.
Your phone turned “Report is done” into “Report is dumb.” Your boss has a sense of humor. Or not. Find out?
In the morning you realize you signed every email to the boss yesterday “Your’s truly.” With the apostrophe. Eight emails.
You sent the boss a link to a document, but pasted the wrong one: instead of the report, “Best Cat Fails” video. He already opened it.
In the work chat you called the boss “Ivan Ivanovich.” He’s Ivan Petrovich. Everyone saw.
In the morning the boss replies: “Thanks, but I’m Sergei, not Sergai.” You reread your email: “Dear Sergai.”
The boss holds up your email as an example to the department: “This is how you write.” It has two typos, and you can see them. Stay quiet?
Your status in the work chat this morning: “Working on the reprot.” It’s been up since Monday. It’s Wednesday. Has anyone noticed?
right: Keep it as your signature style

text: You write the boss “I’m in a meeting” and send “I’m in a meating.” He replies: “Where’s the meating?”
Autocorrect turned “Can we discuss at 11?” into “Can we discuss at age 11?” The boss replied: “Let’s make it sooner.”
You sent the boss an email reading “Please approve. Do not approve.” It’s a leftover from your draft.
You write the boss: “The file’s in your inbox.” No attachment. The boss replies: “Where?” You attach the wrong one.
You mixed up recipients: “How do I politely say no to my boss?” went to your boss. A minute later he writes: “Want some tips?”
right: Say it’s about an old job

text: Instead of “Done, please check,” you sent the boss “Done, please check” plus a dancing potato sticker. Your finger missed.
The boss sent you a document riddled with typos and asked you to “check the spelling.” There are 64 errors. Fix them all?
You sent an important email to the boss and only then noticed the subject says “Proposla” instead of “Proposal.” He hasn’t opened it yet.
The boss asks for a client’s number. You sent it, but swapped two digits. The boss already called. He reached a pizzeria.
In your email to the boss you wrote “Best regards” and forgot to finish your name. It reads “Best regards, a.” Sent.
left: Finish it in a new email

text: Lena sends you an email she’s about to send to the boss. The first line says “Good afternon” instead of “Good afternoon.” Tell her?
6:10 p.m. You sent the boss the final report, and the first line reads: “Final report (not final).” It was a note to yourself.
In the evening you text the boss: “Will be in at 9 tomorrow.” Autocorrect changed it to “at 7 p.m. tomorrow.” The boss replied: “OK.”
Your vacation request email came out wrong: “Please release me in August.” It sounds like a desperate plea.
In the evening you meant to text Mom “Love you, kisses,” but sent it to the boss. The boss replies: “Likewise. Report by morning.”
Rereading your email to the boss in the evening, you see: “I commit to delivering everything by Friday.” You meant “I’ll try.” The commitment’s been made.
You sent the boss a voice message you accidentally recorded at the store. You can hear yourself haggling over a cucumber discount. Delete it?
In the evening you realize your email to the boss said “by Tuesday” instead of “by Thursday.” The boss has already put it in his calendar.
Before bed you remember signing an email to the boss “Regards, your kitty.” It was your personal email signature. You can’t sleep.
You replied “Ok” to the boss’s message “Are you fired?” — he meant “Are you tired?” Now you’re both afraid to continue.
right: Say: “Ok as in, full of energy”

text: In the evening you sent the boss a spreadsheet with the comment: “This mistake isn’t mine, it’s Petya’s.” Petya is cc’d.
In the evening the boss writes: “Pay attention to the commas in your emails.” No examples. You start rechecking every email from the past month.
right: Sign up for a punctuation course

text: In the evening you accidentally sent the boss an email reading “Stop pestering me, I’m not a robot,” which you’d written just to vent. You meant to delete it.
left: Talk to him in person, fast

text: You sent the boss “Have a nice evening!” with a typo: “Have a nice evning!” He replied: “You too, have a nice evning.”
In the evening you emailed the boss and “key clients” turned into “keg clients.” The email went to finance too.
right: Say it’s a term of art

text: In the evening Vanya sends a screenshot: “Your report to the boss spells it ’qaurter.’” The report is already on the director’s desk.
right: Thank him and let it go

text: In the evening you mean to write “You’re all done, I’m off!” in the work chat, but send just “You’re all done.” The chat freezes. The boss posts a question mark.
In the evening you learn the boss printed your typo-filled email and pinned it to the board labeled “Training example.”
left: Ask him to take it down

text: In the evening you reread everything you sent the boss today. Every third message has a typo. Sign up for a typing course?
You sent the boss a report named “Report_midnight_nonsense.docx.” The name was left over from the draft. Sent at 9 p.m.
In the evening you write the boss “Thanks for your patience,” but autocorrect adds “and dumplings.” There were no dumplings.
In the evening the boss sends back your own email with every error highlighted in red. At the bottom: “Great job, but...” Reply?
The budget that went to the boss has an extra zero: $1,000,000 instead of $100,000. The boss already forwarded the file to the director. What now?
You write the boss “I’ll think about your proposal,” then send “I’ll think about your proposal” plus a photo of your dinner.
You replied to the boss without reading his email to the end. The last line asked: “Can you come in on Saturday?” You answered “Of course!”
Danya asks in the evening: “Did you call the boss ’Your Majesty’ in the team chat?” Autocorrect turned “your vision” into that.
In the evening you texted the boss “Will have it by 9 a.m.,” though you meant “9 p.m.” — and it’s already 9 p.m. The boss replied: “Great, see it in the morning.”
You sent the boss a request for a day off dated “February 31.” The boss approved it. Is that a joke, or did he not read it?
In the evening you write the boss “Everything’s under control,” but it comes out “under contol.” He replies: “Then all is well.”
You realize that for a whole month you’ve signed emails “Sales Manger” instead of “Sales Manager.” The boss said nothing.
In the evening you resolve never to message the boss again without spellcheck. At 11:40 p.m. he texts: “Still up?”
In the evening you write in the work chat “Boss, you’re a genius!” — it was meant for a coworker, but you mixed up names. The boss is delighted.
You sent the boss an email ending with “P.S. don’t forget to buy cat food.” It was a note to yourself.
You sent the boss a photo of a document, but your reflection in pajamas is visible in a mirror. Sent at 10:15 p.m.
In the evening you see your email to the boss went out in size-48 font. Every word is as big as your palm on screen.
Alisa writes in the evening: “The boss quoted your email at the meeting today. There was a typo in ’strategy.’” You weren’t at the meeting.
7:30 p.m. Someone in the team chat asks if a laptop charger was left at the office. You’re home, and the charger is yours, in your bag. Own up?
The evening call ended, but you forgot to leave. Half an hour later two coworkers join the same room and discuss your report. They’re praising it. Reveal yourself?
8:10 p.m. Your laptop says your access certificate expired today. Support closes at 6 p.m. Tomorrow at 9:00 you present from your laptop.
In the evening you notice it’s the third day in a row you’re eating dinner at your work desk in front of your open inbox. The plate is right on the keyboard. Relocate dinner?
Before leaving, a coworker asks you to “close his spreadsheet without saving.” You click the wrong thing, and his changes save over the original. Tell him now?
In the evening the cat sat on the keyboard just as you were sending a report. Your email to the boss now contains the line “zzzzzzxxxx.” Sent.
In the evening the portal notifies you: “Happy anniversary — six months with the company!” Only the portal and your mom congratulated you. Tell coworkers?
